description: Extracting groundwater from aquifers and protecting them from domestic and hazardous waste.
content_html:
What is an Aquifer?

Most of the freshwater people use does not come from rivers or lakes — it comes from underground. An aquifer is a body of rock that is both porous enough to store significant quantities of water and permeable enough to transmit it. The water table marks the upper boundary of the saturated zone — all rock below it has pores filled with water; above it, pores contain mainly air. Where the water table meets the surface, a natural spring forms. Wells are simply boreholes drilled down to or below the water table to extract groundwater.

Two properties govern whether a rock makes a good aquifer: porosity (how much water it can store) and permeability (how readily water moves through it). Chalk is one of the most important aquifers in the UK — it has moderate porosity in its primary pores and is highly permeable along its extensive fracture and joint networks. The Chalk aquifer underlies much of south-east England and supplies drinking water to millions of people. Sandstone aquifers (such as the Triassic Sherwood Sandstone of the English Midlands) have high primary porosity in inter-grain pore spaces.

Key Fact

A good aquifer must be both porous (to store water) and permeable (to allow water to flow to a well). A rock with high porosity but low permeability — like clay — can hold water but will not yield it fast enough to supply a well. A rock with high permeability but low porosity holds too little water to be useful.

Domestic Waste and Landfill Sites

Every community generates solid waste — household rubbish, garden material, and general commercial refuse. In many areas, this is buried in landfill sites. As rainwater percolates through decomposing waste, it picks up dissolved organic compounds, heavy metals and pathogens, creating a contaminated liquid called leachate. If leachate reaches an aquifer, it can render groundwater unfit for drinking across a wide area — contamination that may persist for decades because groundwater moves slowly and there are few mechanisms to naturally purify it underground.

Modern landfill engineering uses multiple barriers to prevent this. A geomembrane — a thick plastic liner — is laid beneath and around the waste. On top of this sits a layer of compacted clay, which has very low permeability and provides a second seal. Leachate is collected in drainage pipes and pumped to a treatment facility. Monitoring boreholes around the perimeter of the site routinely sample groundwater so that any breach of the liner is detected quickly.

Regulators and planners avoid siting landfills over or near major aquifers, particularly where the aquifer is unconfined (directly connected to the surface with no overlying impermeable layer). A confined aquifer — one overlain by an impermeable layer such as clay — is more protected, but contamination from a landfill above the confining layer could still migrate laterally. The Environment Agency uses geological maps from the British Geological Survey to classify land as ‘source protection zones’ around boreholes and springs that supply public drinking water. The innermost zone (Zone 1, the ‘inner protection zone’) has the strictest restrictions on development and industrial activity.

Hazardous Waste and Geological Disposal

Some waste is far more dangerous than household refuse: radioactive material from nuclear power plants, toxic industrial chemicals, and contaminated sludge from processing facilities. The geological disposal of hazardous waste uses the Earth's rock as a long-term barrier. The key requirement is a aquitard (sometimes called a confining layer) — a tight, impermeable formation through which groundwater cannot migrate and waste cannot escape.

Critically, the most porous and permeable rocks — sandstones and limestones that make good aquifers — are the worst choices for waste disposal. Waste placed in them would rapidly dissolve into and spread through the groundwater system. Instead, geologists favour massive, unfractured mudstones, evaporites (rock salt) or stable crystalline basement rocks such as granite for waste isolation. The Geological Disposal Facility planned for the UK's higher-activity radioactive waste will be sited hundreds of metres below the surface in stable host rock, using a combination of engineered barriers and the natural geology to contain radionuclides for thousands of years.

Key Fact

Good aquifer rocks (porous and permeable sandstone, limestone) are dangerous for waste disposal because contaminants migrate rapidly through them into drinking water supplies. Impermeable rocks such as unfractured mudstone, massive halite or granite are preferred for waste isolation because fluids cannot pass through them.

Once groundwater contamination has occurred, remediation is difficult and expensive. Monitoring wells placed downgradient (in the direction of groundwater flow) from a contaminated site detect whether a plume of pollutants is spreading. Options for remediation include pump-and-treat systems (pumping contaminated water to the surface for treatment before returning clean water), permeable reactive barriers (trenches filled with material that chemically treats contaminants as groundwater flows through), and in some cases bioremediation using microorganisms to break down organic pollutants. All of these are slow and expensive, reinforcing why prevention through careful site selection and engineered containment is far preferable.

Vulnerable Aquifers

Some aquifers are more vulnerable to contamination than others. Unconfined aquifers — where the water table is directly connected to the surface without an overlying impermeable layer — are at greatest risk. The Chalk aquifer in southern England is an example: its well-developed joint and fracture network means that contaminants can travel rapidly from the surface to the water table without the natural filtering that fine-grained soils provide. Over-abstraction (extracting water faster than it is replenished by rainfall) is a second threat: it lowers the water table, causes land subsidence, and in coastal areas can draw salt water into the aquifer in a process called saline intrusion.
exam_tip_html: Examiners frequently set questions where students incorrectly apply oil-field terms to aquifer questions — do not call a permeable limestone a ‘reservoir rock’ or a shale above it a ‘cap rock’ in a water context. In a waste question, the most common error is recommending a porous sandstone for hazardous waste disposal because it has ‘lots of space’ — that is exactly wrong. High porosity and permeability mean rapid contamination of groundwater. For “explain” questions on landfill safety, describe the geomembrane, the clay liner and the monitoring boreholes as three separate points.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • An aquifer is a porous and permeable body of rock that stores and transmits groundwater; the water table marks the top of the saturated zone, and springs form where it reaches the surface.
  • Landfill sites are engineered with geomembranes and clay liners to prevent leachate contaminating aquifers; monitoring boreholes detect any breach early.
  • Rocks suitable for aquifers (high porosity and permeability) are the worst choices for hazardous waste disposal; impermeable mudstone, halite or granite are preferred to prevent contaminant migration.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following rock types would make the best host for a hazardous waste disposal facility?
A) Permeable sandstone
B) Fractured limestone
C) Massive unfractured mudstone
D) Chalk with well-developed joint networks
Name the synthetic liner placed beneath a landfill site to prevent leachate escaping into the ground.
Describe what the water table is and explain how it relates to the formation of natural springs.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark each for:
- The water table is the upper surface of the zone of saturated rock in an aquifer, below which all pore spaces are filled with water. (1)
- Where the water table intersects the ground surface — for example, on a hillside or in a valley — groundwater discharges naturally as a spring. (1)

practice_questions.text: A monitoring borehole records a groundwater nitrate concentration of 12 mg/L in January. By August, the concentration has risen to 48 mg/L. Calculate the percentage increase in nitrate concentration. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Percentage increase = ((48 - 12) / 12) × 100 = (36 / 12) × 100 = 300%
[2 marks: 1 for correct method, 1 for correct answer]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a porous and permeable sandstone is a poor choice for the geological disposal of hazardous waste.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
- Sandstone has high porosity, meaning it contains large pore spaces that the waste or its dissolved components would occupy. (1)
- Its high permeability means groundwater flows readily through it; any waste or leachate would be transported rapidly away from the disposal site by moving groundwater. (1)
- Contamination would spread widely into the groundwater system, potentially reaching wells and springs that supply drinking water far from the disposal site before detection. (1)

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the geological factors that determine whether a site is suitable for a domestic landfill. In your answer, consider both the rock type and the position relative to aquifers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Discusses rock permeability, aquifer vulnerability, confining layers, water table depth and monitoring; recognises the multi-factor nature of siting decisions; reaches a justified conclusion.
Secure: At least three geological factors discussed with explanations; conclusion present.
Developing: Identifies relevant factors but explanation is limited; conclusion may be absent.
Emerging: Names one or two factors without explanation.

Key factors:
- Underlying rock must have low permeability to reduce leachate migration risk; clay or dense mudstone beneath the site provides a natural barrier even before engineered liners are added.
- The site should not overlie a major unconfined aquifer; the Chalk in south-east England, for example, has highly developed fracture networks that transmit contaminants rapidly, making it a high-risk host.
- A confining layer (impermeable stratum) between the landfill base and any aquifer below adds natural protection; the greater the thickness and continuity of this layer, the safer the site.
- The water table must be deep enough below the base of the waste to provide a buffer zone; a site where the water table is within a few metres of the surface is high risk.
- The regional groundwater flow direction matters: monitoring boreholes should be placed downgradient; any breach will move in that direction.
- Proximity to Source Protection Zones (inner zones around public water supply boreholes) should disqualify a site.

Conclusion: No single geological factor is decisive; siting decisions require combining rock permeability, aquifer classification, water table depth and groundwater flow direction into a holistic assessment. The most important principle is to maximise the natural geological barrier between the waste and any usable groundwater, and to supplement this with engineered barriers and long-term monitoring. [6 marks]

options: The depth at which all pore spaces in the rock are filled with air
The upper surface of the zone of saturated rock in an aquifer
The boundary between an aquifer and an underlying impermeable rock
The level at which a borehole must be drilled to reach oil

knowledge_checks.q: Why is chalk considered a vulnerable aquifer in southern England?
options: It has very high clay content that absorbs contaminants
Its well-developed fracture and joint network allows rapid transport of pollutants from the surface
It lies too deep for contamination from surface sources to reach
It has very low porosity and therefore holds little water

knowledge_checks.q: Rainwater percolating through decomposing landfill waste produces a contaminated liquid called _____.
A _____ is a synthetic plastic liner placed beneath a landfill to prevent leachate from escaping into the ground.
Match each rock type to its suitability for water or waste geology:
right: Good aquifer — high primary porosity yields water to wells readily
Preferred waste disposal host — very low permeability prevents fluid migration
Vulnerable aquifer — fractures allow rapid surface-to-water-table transport

flashcard_questions.a: A body of permeable rock that stores and transmits groundwater, extractable via wells or discharged as springs.
The upper surface of the saturated zone in an aquifer, below which all pore spaces are filled with water.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two UK aquifer rock types.
flashcard_questions.a: Chalk (south-east England) and Triassic Sherwood Sandstone (English Midlands).

flashcard_questions.q: What is leachate and why is it dangerous?
flashcard_questions.a: Contaminated liquid produced as rainwater percolates through decomposing landfill waste; it can pollute aquifers.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a geomembrane in landfill engineering?
flashcard_questions.a: A synthetic plastic liner placed beneath landfill waste to prevent leachate from escaping into the ground.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is a porous sandstone a poor host rock for hazardous waste?
flashcard_questions.a: High permeability means contaminants migrate rapidly through groundwater, spreading pollution widely.

flashcard_questions.q: What rock type is preferred for geological disposal of radioactive waste?
flashcard_questions.a: Massive unfractured mudstone, rock salt (halite) or stable granite — all with very low permeability.

flashcard_questions.q: What is saline intrusion in a coastal aquifer?
flashcard_questions.a: Over-abstraction lowers the water table, drawing salt water inland into the freshwater aquifer.

flashcard_questions.q: What is an unconfined aquifer and why is it more vulnerable to contamination?
flashcard_questions.a: An aquifer directly connected to the surface with no overlying impermeable layer, so pollutants can reach it quickly.

flashcard_questions.q: What are monitoring boreholes used for at a landfill site?
flashcard_questions.a: To regularly sample groundwater around the site and detect any breach of the liner before contamination spreads.

glossary_terms.definition: A body of permeable rock that holds and transmits groundwater, which can be extracted from wells or that discharges naturally as springs.
The upper surface of the zone of saturated rock in an aquifer, below which all pore spaces are filled with water.
A site where waste is buried in the ground in layers, engineered to contain leachate and prevent groundwater contamination.
A synthetic liner made of high-density polyethylene or similar material, placed beneath a landfill to prevent leachate from escaping into the ground.
A rock that has very low permeability and prevents fluid movement, making it suitable for isolating hazardous waste from groundwater.
Easily contaminated by pollutants at the surface because there is little or no natural geological protection between the land surface and the water table.
